Content:
When simplifying an algebraic expression involving square roots, it's useful to remember that

Content:
[MATH: \sqrt{x^2} = |x|.]

Content:
It's tempting to think that [MATH: \sqrt{x^2}] is equivalent to [MATH: x,] but that's not true because [MATH: \sqrt{x^2}] is always non-negative, even if [MATH: x] is negative.

Content:
To illustrate, let's evaluate [MATH: \sqrt{x^2}] for a couple of different values of [MATH: x\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: sqrt(4^{2})|= sqrt(16) = 4; sqrt((− 4)^{2})|= sqrt(16) = 4]

Content:
In both cases, using absolute value gives the correct result:

Content:
[MATH: sqrt(4^{2}) =|4||= 4|✓; sqrt((− 4)^{2}) =|− 4||= 4|✓]

items.title: Expressing the Square Root of a Perfect Square Using Absolute Value

key_prerequisites.name: The Square Root of a Perfect Square

sections.normalized_html:
Remember that the square root of a perfect square can be simplified using absolute value.

[MATH: \sqrt{x^2} = |x|]

Also, we notice that [MATH: 16] and [MATH: y^2] are both perfect squares.

First, we write the expression under the square root as a perfect square:

[MATH: sqrt(16y^{2})|= sqrt(4^{2} ⋅ y^{2}); = sqrt(4 ⋅ 4 ⋅ y ⋅ y); = sqrt(4 ⋅ y ⋅ 4 ⋅ y); = sqrt(4y ⋅ 4y); = sqrt((4y)^{2})]

Then, we take the absolute value of the squared quantity and simplify using the rules of absolute value:

[MATH: sqrt((4y)^{2})|=|4y|; =|4|⋅|y|; = 4|y|]
